The '''Rocq Prover''' (formerly named '''Coq''') is an [[proof assistant|interactive theorem prover]] first released in 1989. It allows the expression of mathematical assertions, mechanical checking of proofs of these assertions, assists in finding [[formal proof]]s using proof automation routines and extraction of a certified program from the [[constructive proof]] of its [[formal specification]]. 

Rocq works within the theory of the calculus of inductive constructions, a derivative of the [[calculus of constructions]]. Rocq is not an [[automated theorem prover]] but includes automatic theorem proving tactics ([[Subroutine|procedures]]) and various [[Decidability (logic)|decision]] procedures.

The [[Association for Computing Machinery]] awarded [[Thierry Coquand]], [[Gérard Huet]], [[Christine Paulin-Mohring]], Bruno Barras, Jean-Christophe Filliâtre, Hugo Herbelin, Chetan Murthy, Yves Bertot, and Pierre Castéran with the 2013 [[ACM Software System Award]] for Rocq (when it was named Coq).

== Overview ==
When viewed as a [[programming language]], Rocq implements a [[dependent type|dependently typed]] [[functional programming]] model;<ref>[https://rocq-prover.org/docs/tour-of-rocq A Tour of Rocq]</ref> when viewed as a logical system, it implements a [[higher-order logic|higher-order]] [[type theory]]. The development of Rocq has been supported since 1984 by [[French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation]] (INRIA), in collaboration with many other French and international research institutions. The development of Rocq was initiated by Gérard Huet and Thierry Coquand, and more than 200 people,<ref>[https://rocq-prover.org/about#history A Brief History]</ref> mainly researchers, have contributed features to the core system since its inception. The implementation team has successively been coordinated by Gérard Huet, Christine Paulin-Mohring, Hugo Herbelin, and Matthieu Sozeau. Rocq is mainly implemented in [[OCaml]] with a bit of [[C (programming language)|C]]. The core system can be extended by way of a [[Plug-in (computing)|plug-in]] mechanism.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Avigad |first1=Jeremy |last2=Mahboubi |first2=Assia |title=Interactive Theorem Proving: 9th International Conference, ITP 2018, Held as ... |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=I-tiDwAAQBAJ&q=%22coq%22,%22plugins%22,%22extended%22&pg=PA21 |date=3 July 2018 |publisher=Springer |isbn=9783319948218 |access-date=21 October 2018}}</ref>

Rocq provides a specification language named Gallina.<ref>
{{cite book |last1=Chlipala |first1=Adam |date=7 June 2022 |url=http://adam.chlipala.net/cpdt/html/Universes.html |chapter=Library Universes |title=Certified Programming with Dependent Types: A Pragmatic Introduction to the Coq Proof Assistant |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |isbn=978-0262026659}}</ref> 
Programs written in Gallina have the [[Normalization property (abstract rewriting)|weak normalization]] property, implying that they always terminate.
This is a distinctive property of the language, since infinite loops (non-terminating programs) are common in other programming languages.<ref>
Adam Chlipala.
"Certified Programming with Dependent Types":
[http://adam.chlipala.net/cpdt/html/GeneralRec.html "Library GeneralRec"].
[http://adam.chlipala.net/cpdt/html/InductiveTypes.html "Library InductiveTypes"].
</ref>

As an example of a proof written in Rocq, consider a proof of a lemma which states that taking the successor of a natural number flips its parity. The fold-unfold tactic introduced by Danvy<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Danvy |first=Olivier |date=2022 |title=Fold–unfold lemmas for reasoning about recursive programs using the Coq proof assistant |journal=Journal of Functional Programming |language=en |volume=32 |doi=10.1017/S0956796822000107 |issn=0956-7968|doi-access=free}}</ref> is used to help keep the proof simple.<syntaxhighlight lang="coq">
From Stdlib Require Import Arith Nat Bool.

Fixpoint is_even (n : nat) : bool :=
  match n with
  | 0 => true
  | S n' => negb (is_even n')
  end.

Lemma is_even_0 :
  is_even 0 = true.
Proof. reflexivity. Qed.

Lemma is_even_S n :
  is_even (S n) = negb (is_even n).
Proof. reflexivity. Qed.

Lemma successor_flips_evenness n :
  is_even n = negb (is_even (S n)).
Proof.
  rewrite is_even_S.
  destruct (is_even n).
  * simpl. reflexivity.
  * simpl. reflexivity.
Qed.
</syntaxhighlight>

This proof firsts import the definition of booleans and natural numbers from the standard library, and then defines a <code>is_even</code> which is a function returning whether a number is even. Then, three lemmas are proven about this function. The first just restate the defining equations of <code>is_even</code>, and since Rocq knows the equations their proof is very short. The last lemma is proven with a case distinction after first applying the second lemma; the star <code>*</code> demarks that a new sub-case starts there. 

==Notable uses==
===Four color theorem and SSReflect extension===
[[Georges Gonthier]] of [[Microsoft Research]] in [[Cambridge]], [[England]] and Benjamin Werner of [[French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation|INRIA]] used Rocq to create a [[Non-surveyable proof|surveyable proof]] of the [[four color theorem]], which was completed in 2002.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Gonthier |first=Georges |title=Formal Proof—The Four-Color Theorem |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=55 |year=2008|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200811/tx081101382p.pdf |issue=11 |pages=1382–1393 |mr=2463991}}</ref>  Their work led to the development of the SSReflect ("Small Scale Reflection") package, which was a significant extension to Rocq.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gonthier |first1=Georges |last2=Mahboubi |first2=Assia |doi=10.6092/ISSN.1972-5787/1979 |issue=2 |journal=Journal of Formalized Reasoning |pages=95–152 |title=An introduction to small scale reflection in Coq |url=https://jfr.unibo.it/article/view/1979 |volume=3 |year=2010}}</ref> Despite its name, most of the features added to Rocq by SSReflect are general-purpose features and are not limited to the computational [[reflective programming]] style of proof. These features include:

* Added convenient notations for irrefutable and refutable [[pattern matching]], on [[inductive type]]s with one or two constructors
* Implicit arguments for functions applied to zero arguments, which is useful when programming with [[higher-order function]]s
* Concise anonymous arguments
* An improved <code>set</code> tactic with more powerful matching
* Support for reflection

SSReflect is distributed as part of the main Rocq distribution since Coq 8.7.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V9.0.0/refman/changes.html#version-8-7 |title=Version 8.7 Summary of changes|website=rocq-prover.org}}</ref>

==Other applications==

{{See also|Proof assistant#Notable formalized proofs}}

*[[CompCert]]: an optimizing compiler for almost all of the [[C (programming language)|C programming language]] which is largely programmed and proven correct in Rocq.
*[[Disjoint-set data structure#History|Disjoint-set data structure]]: correctness proof in Rocq was published in 2007.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Conchon |first1=Sylvain |last2=Filliâtre |first2=Jean-Christophe |editor1-last=Russo |editor1-first=Claudio V. |editor2-last=Dreyer |editor2-first=Derek |contribution=A persistent union-find data structure |doi=10.1145/1292535.1292541 |pages=37–46 |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |title=Proceedings of the ACM Workshop on ML, 2007, Freiburg, Germany, October 5, 2007 |url=https://www.lri.fr/~filliatr/puf/ |year=2007|isbn=978-1-59593-676-9 }}</ref>
*[[Feit–Thompson theorem]]: formal proof using Rocq was completed in September 2012.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.msr-inria.fr/news/feit-thomson-proved-in-coq/ |title=Feit-Thompson theorem has been totally checked in Coq |publisher=Msr-inria.inria.fr |date=2012-09-20 |access-date=2012-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161119094854/http://www.msr-inria.fr/news/feit-thomson-proved-in-coq/ |archive-date=2016-11-19 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
*[[Busy beaver]]: The value of the 5-state winning busy beaver was discovered by Heiner Marxen and Jürgen Buntrock in 1989, but only proved to be the winning fifth busy beaver — stylized as '''BB(5)''' — in 2024 using a proof in Rocq.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-02 |title=[July 2nd 2024] We have proved "BB(5) = 47,176,870" |url=https://discuss.bbchallenge.org/t/july-2nd-2024-we-have-proved-bb-5-47-176-870/237 |access-date=2024-07-02 |website=The Busy Beaver Challenge |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Busy Beaver Challenge |url=https://bbchallenge.org/ |access-date=2024-07-02 |website=bbchallenge.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Tactic language==

In addition to constructing Gallina terms explicitly, Rocq supports the use of ''tactics'' written in the built-in language Ltac or in OCaml. These tactics automate the construction of proofs, carrying out trivial or obvious steps in proofs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kaiser |first1=Jan-Oliver |last2=Ziliani |first2=Beta |last3=Krebbers |first3=Robbert |last4=Régis-Gianas |first4=Yann |last5=Dreyer |first5=Derek |date=2018-07-30 |title=Mtac2: typed tactics for backward reasoning in Coq |journal=Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages |volume=2 |issue=ICFP |pages=78:1–78:31 |doi=10.1145/3236773|doi-access=free |hdl=21.11116/0000-0003-2E8E-B |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Several tactics implement decision procedures for various theories. For example, the "ring" tactic decides the theory of equality modulo [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] or [[semiring]] axioms via [[Associative property|associative]]-[[Commutative property|commutative]] rewriting.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Grégoire |first1=Benjamin |last2=Mahboubi |first2=Assia |date=2005 |editor-last=Hurd |editor-first=Joe |editor2-last=Melham |editor2-first=Tom |contribution=Proving Equalities in a Commutative Ring Done Right in Coq |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11541868_7 |title= Theorem Proving in Higher Order Logics: 18th International Conference, TPHOLs 2005, Oxford, UK, August 22–25, 2005, Proceedings |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=98–113 |doi=10.1007/11541868_7 |isbn=978-3-540-31820-0}}</ref> For example, the following proof establishes a complex equality in the ring of [[integer]]s in just one line of proof:<ref>{{Cite web |title=The ring and field tactic families — Rocq Prover 9.0.0 documentation |url=https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V9.0.0/refman/addendum/ring.html |access-date=2025-05-07 |website=rocq-prover.org}}</ref>

<syntaxhighlight lang="coq">
Require Import ZArith.
Open Scope Z_scope.
Goal forall a b c:Z,
    (a + b + c) ^ 2 =
     a * a + b ^ 2 + c * c + 2 * a * b + 2 * a * c + 2 * b * c.
  intros; ring.
Qed.
</syntaxhighlight>

Built-in decision procedures are also available for the [[empty theory]] ("congruence"), propositional logic ("tauto"), quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic ("lia"), and linear rational/real arithmetic ("lra").<ref>{{Cite book |last=Besson |first=Frédéric |date=2007 |editor-last=Altenkirch |editor-first=Thorsten |editor2-last=McBride |editor2-first=Conor |chapter=Fast Reflexive Arithmetic Tactics the Linear Case and Beyond |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-74464-1_4 |title=Types for Proofs and Programs: International Workshop, TYPES 2006, Nottingham, UK, April 18–21, 2006, Revised Selected Papers |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=4502 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=48–62 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-74464-1_4 |isbn=978-3-540-74464-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Micromega: solvers for arithmetic goals over ordered rings — Rocq Prover 9.0.0 documentation |url=https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V9.0.0/refman/addendum/micromega.html |access-date=2025-05-07 |website=rocq-prover.org}}</ref> Further decision procedures have been developed as libraries, including one for [[Kleene algebra]]s<ref>{{Cite conference |last1=Braibant |first1=Thomas |last2=Pous |first2=Damien |date=2010 |editor-last=Kaufmann |editor-first=Matt |editor2-last=Paulson |editor2-first=Lawrence C. |title=An Efficient Coq Tactic for Deciding Kleene Algebras |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-14052-5_13 |conference=Interactive Theorem Proving: |date=2004 |editor-last=Slind |editor-first=Konrad |editor2-last=Bunker |editor2-first=Annette |editor3-last=Gopalakrishnan |editor3-first=Ganesh |chapter=A Decision Procedure for Geometry in Coq |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-30142-4_17 |title=Theorem Proving in Higher Order Logics: 17th International Conference, TPHOLS 2004, Park City, Utah, USA, September ==Name==

[[File:Coq logo.png|thumb|Former logo]]

The old name ''{{Lang|fr|[[wikt:coq#French|Coq]]}}'' means '[[rooster]]' in [[French language|French]] and  is a wordplay on the name of Thierry Coquand, ''calculus of constructions'' or ''CoC'', and stems from a French tradition of naming research development tools after animals.<ref>{{cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions |website=[[GitHub]] |url=https://github.com/coq/coq/wiki/Presentation |access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> Until 1991, Coquand was implementing a language named the ''[[calculus of constructions]]'' and it was simply called ''CoC'' then. In 1991, a new implementation based on the extended ''calculus of inductive constructions'' was begun and the name changed from ''CoC'' to ''Coq'' in an indirect reference to Coquand, who developed the ''calculus of constructions'' along with Gérard Huet and contributed to the ''calculus of inductive constructions'' with Christine Paulin-Mohring.<ref>{{cite web |title=Introduction to the Calculus of Inductive Constructions |url=https://hal.inria.fr/hal-01094195/document |access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref> On October 11, 2023, the development team announced that ''Coq'' would be renamed ''The Rocq Prover'' in coming months, and began updating the code base, website, and related tools.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Coq roadmap 069 |website=[[GitHub]] |url=https://github.com/coq/ceps/blob/coq-roadmap/text/069-coq-roadmap.md#change-of-name-coq---the-rocq-prover}}</ref> The official renaming happened with the release of Rocq 9.0 in March 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Version 9.0 Summary of changes |website=rocq-prover.org |url=https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V9.0.0/refman/changes.html#version-9-0}}</ref> The new name refers to [[French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation|Inria Rocquencourt]], where the system was developed first, and is related to the mythical bird [[Roc (mythology)|Roc]], which allows keeping the bird references from the prior name.<ref>{{Cite web |title=An Overview of the Name's Evolution |website=rocq-prover.org |url=https://rocq-prover.org/about#Name}}</ref>
